name: Snakes
label: Dischord
lede: Two Georgetown kids from SOA made a goofy pop record so far from hardcore that Dischord put it out under a fake label name, then came back for a second one five years later.

eras.title: A private joke under the hardcore
eras.text: Michael Hampton and Simon Jacobsen grew up together in Georgetown, and the Snakes ran underneath everything else they did. Dischord says the band both predated and co-existed with their hardcore bands.

years.h: Hampton and Jacobsen are already the Snakes before anyone hears of SOA
years.p: [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]] and [[Simon Jacobsen|59d87a31-7ad6-418f-bee0-5a4738acf357]] have the Snakes going in Georgetown by the time they start playing in The Extorts, Hampton's first band on record.

years.cap: Hampton with the Faith at the Chancery, Washington DC, 1982
years.h: Hampton and Jacobsen play on SOA's No Policy
years.p: Dischord No. 2 is fronted by Henry Garfield, a year before he's [[Henry Rollins|656b39fb-979c-4c57-bb87-61d1a8eb38d1]]. Hampton moves on to [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]] with [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]].
years.xp:
Bandcamp Daily's Tony Rettman traces the Snakes back to this record: Hampton on guitar, Jacobsen on drums, on the label's second release.

It's the obvious contrast. SOA plays fast and aggressive; the Snakes, in Rettman's word, are "downright playful."

eras.title: Dischord, briefly Discard
eras.text: 1985 was Revolution Summer, the most earnest season DC punk ever had. Dischord picked that year to release fourteen songs of playful, proto-punk-flavored pop, and got nervous enough to change its own name on the sleeve.

yt: I Won't Love You, title track
years.h: I Won't Love You ('Til You're More Like Me) · Dischord No. 18
years.p: Fourteen songs recorded at Inner Ear Studios and produced by [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and the band. Titles include Snake Rap, Serv-Pro Joe and License to Fish.
play: I Won't Love You ('Til You're More Like Me)

years.big: "changed the label name to 'Discard' solely for this release"
years.src: Bandcamp Daily · End On End · Dischord
years.h: Dischord puts the Snakes out as Discard Records
years.p: Bandcamp Daily's Tony Rettman says [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] and Ian MacKaye worried how a playful record would land from a hardcore label.
years.xp:
Rettman hears the sound as proto-punk rather than hardcore, in the line of 1960s garage comps like Nuggets and Back From The Grave.

An End On End podcast episode for Dischord's 40th anniversary, with Jacobsen as guest, called the Snakes an anomaly in the scene. Dischord's own page says the band predated and co-existed with Hampton's and Jacobsen's hardcore bands.

years.h: The Snakes play live exactly once, at the 9:30 Club
years.p: It's a recording project. For the one show, at 9:30 Club on F Street NW, two friends Dischord names only as Brendan and Guy back them up.
years.xp: Dischord gives no date for the show. The two backing musicians are listed only by first name.

eras.title: Happy, plus a second disguise
eras.text: Hampton kept moving through the post-Revolution Summer bands while the Snakes stayed a studio habit. Their second album, Happy, came out in 1990, co-released with Adult Swim Records, a small D.C. label.

years.h: Hampton joins One Last Wish after Embrace
years.p: Hampton plays in [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]] with three former members of [[Rites of Spring|b2ff1a6d-9198-4646-b068-8965242d245b]]. Wikipedia says the Snakes carry on alongside, rarely playing live.

years.h: Happy arrives with Adult Swim Records riding along · Dischord No. 50.5
years.p: Thirteen songs, including My Girl Gloria, Oh No, Olga and Dance, Mr. Fish. A listener on Dischord's page calls it catchy bubblegum pop with cheesy keyboards.

years.h: Hampton forms Manifesto with Ivor Hanson and Bert Queiroz
years.p: Manifesto puts out an album and a 7" and gets noticed in the UK.

eras.title: Back in print, on Bandcamp
eras.text: Both Snakes records went out of print, then turned up on Bandcamp and in a new round of Dischord deep-cut lists. Hampton, meanwhile, was playing power pop in Fake Names with a band full of old friends.

years.h: Fake Names puts Hampton back in a band with old friends
years.p: [[Fake Names|a4271e33-8969-4dd8-9e3c-88b269e89fe0]] brings in [[Brian Baker|1fd36abf-e43c-4b01-820b-d7280cc27ea5]], Johnny Temple, Dennis Lyxzén and [[Brendan Canty|8b505ef0-c5a7-4deb-bc32-27c882f3c40e]]. Hampton has also spent years scoring TV, games and film.

years.h: Three hours on the Snakes, with Jacobsen
years.p: End On End's 3-hour-24-minute episode has Jacobsen and Dot Dash bassist Hunter Bennett going through I Won't Love You, as Dischord marks its 40th year.
years.xp: The episode went up December 24, 2020. The show's description promises "stories of DC lore and lore of wild, studious prep school punk rock mischief."

years.h: Bandcamp Daily opens its non-Fugazi Dischord list with the Snakes
years.p: Tony Rettman's 2025 list of Dischord records beyond [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] starts with the band and the story of Dischord becoming Discard.

sources.title: Bandcamp Daily: Beyond Fugazi, Dischord's Hidden Gems (Tony Rettman, 2025)
